prompt: Before any rule set is loaded, what does Bazel itself know how to run?
hint: Teaching it Java is the job of rules_java.

choices.text: Maven's lifecycle phases, in order
choices.why: Phases are Maven's model. Bazel has no lifecycle; it has a graph of targets and the actions that build them.

choices.text: The standard Java layout, src/main/java and src/test/java
choices.why: That convention is Maven's. Bazel compiles exactly the files a target lists in srcs, wherever they are.

choices.text: Actions: commands with declared inputs and outputs
choices.why: Right. Everything else, Java included, is rules that turn targets into such actions.

choices.text: The classes inside each jar on the classpath
choices.why: Bazel treats a jar as a file with a hash. Reading classes is javac's business, inside an action.

prompt: Why can your build take a compiled output from a cache a colleague's build filled?
hint: Think about what the key of an action is made of.

choices.text: Her jar has the same file name and version as yours would
choices.why: Names and versions say nothing about the bytes inside. The key is a hash of every input, so two different sources with the same name would never share it.

choices.text: The remote cache keeps the newest build of each target
choices.why: Newest is not the question. An output is reused only when its action key matches, whenever it was stored.

choices.text: Bazel compares the modification times of the sources
choices.why: Timestamps differ between machines for identical files. Bazel hashes content, which is why the cache works across machines at all.

choices.text: Her action and yours hash to the same key
choices.why: Right. Same sources, jars, flags and JDK give the same key, and every input is declared, so equal keys mean the output would come out the same.

prompt: The code of one target reads a file that the target never declared. What happens when Bazel builds it?

choices.text: It fails everywhere, since the sandbox lacks it
choices.why: Right. The mistake shows up everywhere at once, instead of only on the machine where the file is missing.

choices.text: Compiles on machines that happen to have the file
choices.why: That is the non-hermetic build Bazel exists to prevent: it works on one laptop and fails on the next.

choices.text: Adds the file to the declared inputs for you
choices.why: Bazel never guesses inputs. A guess would make the key depend on what a machine happened to contain.

choices.text: Compiles it, but leaves the file out of the action key
choices.why: That would be the worst outcome, a cache serving stale outputs, and the sandbox is there so it cannot happen.

prompt: Which of these go into the action key of a compile action? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The source file being compiled
choices.why: Right. Change one character and the key changes.

choices.text: The time at which the build started
choices.why: If the clock were an input, no key would ever repeat and nothing could be cached.

choices.text: The jar the source compiles against
choices.why: Right. A new version of the library is a new input, so the code is compiled again.

choices.text: The javac command line, flags included
choices.why: Right. --java_language_version=25 and 21 produce different classes, so they are different keys.

choices.text: The name of the developer running the build
choices.why: Two developers building the same commit should share outputs; that is the whole point of a remote cache.

choices.text: The JDK that runs the compiler
choices.why: Right. It is a tool, and tools are inputs too, which is why Bazel pins its own.

prompt: A monorepo has 300 modules, most commits touch one of them, and CI spends its time rebuilding and retesting the other 299. Which change attacks that cost directly?
hint: Running work faster is not the same as not running it.

choices.text: Remote execution, so every action runs on a farm of machines
choices.why: That spreads the same work over more machines. It is faster, but the 299 untouched modules are still compiled and tested.

choices.text: A remote cache that every CI job and every developer reads and fills
choices.why: Right. Unchanged actions and test results come back from the cache by their key, so only what the commit reaches is run.

choices.text: A larger CI machine with twice the cores
choices.why: More cores make the same rebuild quicker. The rebuild of untouched code is the cost, and it stays.

choices.text: A separate repository and Maven build for each module
choices.why: It does stop the rebuilds, and loses the one graph across modules: a change to a shared library now has to be released and picked up 299 times.

prompt: What is the one-line .bazelversion file for?
hint: It is read before Bazel itself runs.

choices.text: It is the module's own version, for other modules that depend on it
choices.why: That is the version in module(...) in MODULE.bazel.

choices.text: It lists the versions the rule sets resolved to
choices.why: That is MODULE.bazel.lock, which Bazel writes.

choices.text: It sets the Java version the code is compiled for
choices.why: That is --java_language_version in .bazelrc.

choices.text: It names the Bazel release that Bazelisk downloads and runs
choices.why: Right. It pins Bazel in the repository, as the wrapper pins Gradle.

prompt: Match each file at the top of the project to what it holds.
hint: One of them Bazel writes itself.

pairs.right: the Bazel release the project builds with
the module and the rule sets it depends on
what the dependencies resolved to, with hashes

prompt: Why does every http_jar in MODULE.bazel carry a sha256?
hint: What happens if the server hands over different bytes?

choices.text: So that the jar's own dependencies are fetched as well
choices.why: A hash fetches nothing. That is what Maven does from a pom, and http_jar does not: hence the four extra entries.

choices.text: So that Bazel checks the publisher's signature on the jar
choices.why: A hash proves the bytes are the ones you pinned, not who published them. Signatures are a different check.

choices.text: So that a different file at that address fails the build
choices.why: Right. A replaced jar or a mirror serving something else is refused rather than compiled in.

choices.text: So that Bazel can find the jar in Maven Central by its hash
choices.why: The url finds the jar. The hash is checked after the download.

prompt: Lesson 1's pom has one <dependency> on commons-validator. How many http_jar entries in this lesson's MODULE.bazel stand for it?
hint: The jar itself, and what it depends on.

prompt: In `//src/main/java/com/example/isbn:isbn`, the text before the colon names the ___ that holds the target.
Why does the java_test set use_testrunner = False and name a main_class?
hint: Which JUnit does Bazel's own runner speak?

choices.text: Bazel's own runner speaks only JUnit 4
choices.why: Right. So JUnit's console launcher becomes the main class, and args tell it which class to run.

choices.text: So the test runs outside the sandbox, where JUnit can find its engine
choices.why: The test still runs in the sandbox; the engine is inside the console jar, a declared dependency.

choices.text: Because rules_java cannot compile tests written for JUnit 6
choices.why: It compiled IsbnCheckTest without complaint. Compiling is not the problem; running is.

choices.text: Because a java_test is always run through a main method
choices.why: Normally Bazel supplies the main itself, its JUnit 4 runner. This test replaces it.

prompt: The second `bazel test //...` printed `(cached) PASSED in 2.0s`. What ran?

choices.text: The test, but without compiling it again
choices.why: Executed 0 out of 1 test. The result itself was reused, not only the compile.

choices.text: Nothing: the result came from the cache, as no input had changed
choices.why: Right. The 2.0s is how long the run that produced the cached result took.

choices.text: The test, faster, in the compiler worker kept alive since the last build
choices.why: Workers keep compilers warm. A cached test result needs no process at all.

choices.text: Only the test methods that had failed before
choices.why: None had failed, and Bazel caches a test target as a whole, not method by method.

prompt: After moving a repository to Bazel 9, a BUILD file fails with "no such attribute 'srcs' in 'java_library' rule". What do you check first?
hint: The message names an attribute. The cause is elsewhere in the file.

choices.text: Whether srcs was renamed in the new rules_java
choices.why: srcs is the attribute every Java rule has always had. The message points at it because it is the first one passed.

choices.text: Whether the BUILD file is named BUILD rather than BUILD.bazel
choices.why: Both names make a package; the rule inside it would fail the same way under either.

choices.text: Whether the file loads java_library from rules_java
choices.why: Right. Without the load, the name does not mean the rule from rules_java, and the attributes are unknown to whatever it does mean.

choices.text: Whether IsbnCheck.java is in the same directory as the BUILD file
choices.why: A missing source gives a different error, naming the file. This one fails before any file is looked at.

prompt: Five developers, one Spring Boot service in its own repository, a Maven build of a minute. Should they move to Bazel?
hint: Weigh what it costs against what a minute leaves to save.

choices.text: Yes: a remote cache would make every build instant
choices.why: A one-minute build has little to cache away, and the cache is one more server to run.

choices.text: Yes: hermetic builds catch mistakes Maven lets through
choices.why: They do, and a team that size meets few of them. The price is every jar declared by hash and tooling that expects a pom.

choices.text: No: what it costs buys almost nothing at that size
choices.why: Right. Every dependency by hand, tools built for Maven, and somebody owning the build, to save part of a minute.

choices.text: No: Bazel cannot build a Spring Boot application
choices.why: It can, with rules_java and rules_jvm_external. It is a poor trade here, not an impossible one.

prompt: Which of these situations count in favour of Bazel? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Twenty teams commit to one repository
choices.why: Right. One graph across everybody's code is what Bazel was built for.

choices.text: Java services share Protocol Buffers files with a Go tool and a TypeScript front end
choices.why: Right. Several languages that depend on each other build in one graph instead of three tools glued together.

choices.text: A newcomer must open the project in an IDE with no setup
choices.why: That favours Maven: IDEs open a pom as it is and a Bazel project through a plugin.

choices.text: CI spends most of its time rebuilding code no commit touched
choices.why: Right. A remote cache turns that time into downloads.

choices.text: The project is one library with three dependencies
choices.why: Small and single-language is exactly where Maven's conventions cost least.

prompt: Somebody clones this lesson's project on a new machine and runs `bazel build //...`. Put what happens in order.
hint: Bazel has to exist before it can read MODULE.bazel.
items: Bazelisk reads .bazelversion and downloads that Bazel
A Bazel server starts and stays in the background
rules_java and the jars named in MODULE.bazel are fetched
The compile actions run, each in its own sandbox
trap: The fetch cannot come first: MODULE.bazel is read by Bazel, and Bazel is what Bazelisk downloads.

prompt: A colleague adds `import org.apache.commons.lang3.StringUtils;` to IsbnCheck.java. That jar is in ~/.m2 on her laptop from a Maven project, and she changes nothing else. What does `bazel build //...` do?
hint: What is in the compile action's sandbox?

choices.text: Builds on her laptop, where the jar is, and fails on CI
choices.why: That is how a non-hermetic build behaves. Bazel never looks in ~/.m2; the sandbox holds declared inputs only.

choices.text: Downloads commons-lang3 from Maven Central, as it is a well-known library
choices.why: Nothing is fetched that MODULE.bazel does not name, and with a hash.

choices.text: Builds everywhere, because javac searches the classpath of the JDK
choices.why: The JDK's own classes are there; a third-party jar is not.

choices.text: Fails everywhere until an http_jar and a deps entry declare the jar
choices.why: Right. The same error on every machine, and the fix is two declarations: the download and the dependency.

prompt: Match each piece of lesson 1's Maven build to its counterpart in this lesson's Bazel build.
hint: Scopes become attributes; the output directory becomes a link.
